data.title: China’s TuringQ Beefs Up Quantum Computing Supply Chain With New Packaging and Testing Center
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 23 -- TuringQ, a Chinese leader in photonic quantum computing, has opened an advanced packaging and testing center in the city of Changsha, marking another step in the company’s efforts to build a complete industrial chain, it said.

As well as research, development, and manufacturing, TuringQ now has advanced packaging and testing capabilities, the Shanghai-based company announced on Nov. 20. The first phase of the new center will be fully operational next year.

Under TuringQ’s plan, the firm aims to gradually build stable capabilities in advanced packaging and testing for photonic chips, as well as the manufacturing of core optoelectronic components.

Advanced packaging and testing is a key link between chip production and end-system applications. It is also vital in the process of using laboratory-scale optical quantum computing technology to create products and achieve industrial-scale deployment, the firm said.

Set up in February 2021, TuringQ makes software and hardware products including photon chips, photon computers, and quantum cloud platforms.

It has raised over CNY1 billion (USD150 million) in its first three years through seven funding rounds, at a valuation of about CNY7 billion. Investors include Legend Capital, SAIC Group, and Oriza Seed.

TuringQ’s application to begin pre-initial public offering tutoring was accepted by the Shanghai branch of the China Securities Regulatory Commission in August, indicating that the company is moving toward listing in the Chinese mainland.

Editor: Tom Litting

data.title: China’s Hubei Province Launches Pilot Program to Align Post-PhD Innovation to Industry Needs
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 23 -- A pilot program for postdoctoral innovation groups has been launched in China’s Hubei province, aiming to bridge the gap between academic research and finding real-world industrial solutions in areas such as future industries, cutting-edge materials, and new energy.

The four inaugural consortiums unveiled today focus on embodied intelligence, advanced new materials, brain-computer interfaces, and new energy. They are led respectively by Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan University of Technology, Tongji Hospital, and Hubei Eve Power.

Postdoctoral researchers enrolled in the program will be required to spend at least six months working for companies connected to their research, said Li Yidan, vice director of the Hubei’s human resources and social security department. 

Each consortium will have six to 10 participating entities and will use a “1+N+X” organizational structure. “1” refers to the lead organization, which oversees overall operations; “N” refers to universities and research institutes responsible for academic training and research supervision; and “X” refers to the participating companies, which will provide postdoctoral researchers with practical training opportunities and real-world application scenarios.

The consortiums will run a range of joint initiatives, including recruiting postdoctoral researchers, establishing shared mentor pools, setting up collaborative research projects, arranging industry placements, opening up research resources to members, organizing academic exchanges, and promoting the use and commercialization of research findings in real-world situations.

For example, the brain-computer interface group led will use Tongji Hospital’s clinical resources to turn real needs arising in wards and among patients into research projects for post-PhD researchers. By bringing together medical and engineering expertise, it aims to create a pathway connecting clinical needs with basic research, followed by clinical validation, and eventual industrialization of research results.

Once the four pilot groups have matured, this collaborative model will be expanded to include areas such as integrated circuits, spatiotemporal geographic information, and green shipbuilding, Li said. The plan is for a total of 15 postdoctoral training innovation consortia to be established by the end of 2030.

The move is aimed at building talent training platforms directly on industrial chains and embedding talent development into the process of tackling research projects, Li added. The next step is to build a "challenge-based" research mechanism, where technical problems from across the industrial chain are identified, with researchers taking on the task of solving them.

Editors: Tang Shihua, Tom Litting

data.title: UBS Sees China’s GDP Growing 4.6% in 2027 as Exports, Domestic Demand Play Seesaw
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 23 -- UBS Securities expects China’s economy to grow 4.6 percent in 2027, broadly in line with its estimate for 2026, with exports and domestic demand remaining locked in a “seesaw” relationship.

Strong exports could reduce the urgency for policymakers to boost domestic demand, while prolonged reliance on overseas markets could leave domestic spending and investment weak, according to Song Yu, UBS Securities’ chief China economist.

“If exports fall, domestic demand will have to make up the difference. To secure growth of 4.5 percent or 4.6 percent, domestic demand will definitely need to be stepped up, so there is a seesaw relationship,” Song said at a recent media briefing.

Weak domestic demand makes it harder for companies to earn profits at home, driving them to rely more on exports. Strong export performance, in turn, could reduce the urgency for further domestic demand stimulus, Song noted.

High-Tech Growth and Yuan Outlook

A similar dynamic applies to high-tech industries and traditional sectors. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence and other technologies could boost China's long-term growth potential but also reduce the urgency of support for weaker sectors if overall growth targets remain stable, Song said.

Song remains optimistic about China’s long-term competitiveness in technology and exports, citing its talent, capital, vast domestic market, and market-oriented incentives alongside policy support.

UBS also expects the yuan to strengthen against the US dollar, reaching CNY6.25 per dollar by the end of 2027, according to its economic outlook report.

A larger trade surplus, reduced capital outflows, and self-reinforcing expectations of appreciation could support further gains, Song said. However, a sharp rise in the US dollar could cause the yuan to deviate from that forecast, he cautioned.

Editor: Emmi Laine

data.title: Tencent, ByteDance Tout AI Office App Gains as User Numbers Surge
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 19 -- Chinese tech giants Tencent Holdings and ByteDance have reported strong user growth and substantial revenue from their artificial intelligence office assistants as competition in China's AI productivity market heats up.

Tencent's WorkBuddy had more than 10 million daily active users as of early November, while ByteDance's Doubao Work surpassed eight million, according to figures released yesterday.

Beyond attracting users, both companies are beginning to generate substantial revenue from their AI tools, raising the stakes for rivals including Alibaba Group Holding.

WorkBuddy's annualized revenue, calculated using its latest seven days of sales, has exceeded USD500 million, double that of video-call tool Tencent Meeting, which launched seven years ago, Tencent President Martin Lau said during an earnings conference call yesterday following the release of the company's third-quarter results.

The AI assistant's revenue in the quarter ended in September was also more than five times that of the previous quarter, Lau added.

WorkBuddy consumed an average of more than 100 trillion tokens a day as of early November, making it Tencent's AI application with the highest daily token consumption, the Shenzhen-based company said in its third-quarter earnings report.

ByteDance is also making headway with corporate customers. The Beijing-based company said Doubao Work had generated over CNY2 billion (USD300 million) in annual recurring revenue from businesses within three months of its launch.

Tech Giants Tap Existing Platforms to Expand AI Reach

Rather than building their AI office businesses from scratch, the three companies are tapping their existing platforms to attract users.

ByteDance developed Doubao Work by integrating its Doubao AI assistant with its workplace collaboration platform Lark.

Tencent has leveraged the user base of its WeChat social media application to expand WorkBuddy's reach and incorporated third-party AI models, including DeepSeek, into the assistant.

Alibaba, meanwhile, has been developing its Qwen AI assistant for enterprise customers, drawing on its DingTalk workplace collaboration platform.

The stakes are rising as China's broader AI agent market expands. The market reached CNY80.4 billion (USD12.1 billion) last year, more than doubling from a year earlier, according to a report released by iiMedia Research. It could reach CNY696.8 billion (USD104.5 billion) by 2030, the research firm forecast.

Unlike traditional office software, AI office assistants primarily attract individuals, but enterprise customers offer another avenue for growth, iiMedia noted. Developers could tap both markets by offering lightweight tools to individuals and tailored solutions to businesses, creating multiple revenue streams, the research firm suggested.

Editors: Dou Shicong, Emmi Laine

data.title: China's Power-Hungry AI Data Centers Could Help Ease Grid Strain, Experts Say
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 23 -- China should make artificial intelligence data centers more responsive to electricity supply and demand to ease mounting pressure on the power grid as computing capacity expands, according to industry experts.

By shifting non-urgent computing tasks to periods of abundant renewable electricity and participating in grid demand response programs, data centers could help balance power supply and demand while reducing their own electricity costs, the experts said. Pilot projects in northern and central China have already demonstrated the potential of this approach.

China's computing centers consumed 170 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2025, accounting for less than 2 percent of national power consumption, the National Energy Administration said in May. Electricity use at the country's eight national computing hub nodes grew by an annual average of about 40 percent over the past three years, far outpacing overall electricity demand.

The administration expects computing-related electricity consumption to reach 800 billion kWh by 2030, or around 6 percent of the national total. The projected increase is intensifying the need to coordinate computing workloads with available electricity resources.

China and the United States together account for more than half of global data center electricity consumption, but the two countries are taking different approaches to meeting rising demand, according to industry experts.

The US is pursuing a "supply expansion" strategy, while China is focusing on optimizing existing resources, said Wang Zesen, deputy director of the Power System Research Institute at State Grid Jibei Electric Power Research Institute. China's approach involves integrated computing workload scheduling, direct connections to green electricity supplies, and a "compute follows power" strategy that aligns computing facilities with available energy resources.

Some major US technology companies seek to secure their own electricity supplies, said Liao Yu, deputy director of the Carbon Neutrality Committee at the China-Germany Innovation Alliance. Apple, Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have each established teams of 200 to 300 people dedicated to developing energy solutions, he noted.

In China, computing companies generally rely on the power grid to meet their electricity needs and may not even need in-house energy specialists. But that convenience comes at a cost, Liao warned.

"If every household has a good nanny doing the cooking, the family's own cooking skills will inevitably get rusty," he said.

Grid Connections and Stability Pose Challenges

Pressure on the power grid is already evident. Data centers account for more than 10 percent of electricity consumption in the area served by State Grid Jibei, the power grid operator in northern Hebei province, according to Wang.

Although local governments can attract computing projects and get construction underway relatively quickly, connecting them to substations operating at 220 kilovolts or above takes considerably longer. "Even in the fastest case, you still have to wait at least three to five years," Wang said.

The challenges extend beyond the amount of electricity data centers consume. The large-scale integration of power electronic equipment can also affect grid stability, Wang noted.

Another obstacle is the lack of visibility into data center operations. Grid operators can monitor electricity meters and substations at the other end of a connection, but they cannot see how computing workloads are operating inside individual facilities.

How to share this information among grid operators, computing facility investors, and regulators remains an unresolved issue, Wang said.

The increasing power density of artificial intelligence data centers, or AIDCs, is adding to these challenges. Power requirements per AIDC rack are expected to rise from the traditional range of several kilowatts to tens of kW to the megawatt level, while entire data center campuses could require gigawatts of electricity, according to Wang Jun, director of intelligent industry equipment at NR Electric, a Chinese provider of power grid equipment.

Fluctuations in graphics processing unit inference workloads can occur within milliseconds. Combined with variations in renewable electricity generation, these rapid changes pose additional risks to power system stability, Wang said.

Turning Computing Demand Into Grid Flexibility

Data centers could help ease these pressures by adjusting the timing of certain computing tasks in response to electricity availability and prices, provided service quality and operational safety are maintained.

Such flexibility could also reduce operators' electricity costs. Negative electricity prices have already emerged in places including Shandong and Sichuan during afternoon periods of abundant wind and solar generation, Liao said. Data centers could move non-real-time computing tasks originally scheduled for nighttime into these lower-cost periods.

Data centers could also install their own solar power generation equipment to reduce reliance on grid electricity. Liao likened this to major industrial companies such as Baosteel building their own power plants to meet part of their electricity needs, describing on-site solar facilities as "captive power plants for the green energy era."

As China's electricity retail market becomes more open to competition, data centers could further reduce their power costs by buying electricity under more flexible contracts. Instead of paying a fixed price throughout the year, they could negotiate monthly pricing arrangements with electricity retailers to take advantage of changing market conditions, Liao said.

China has already begun testing coordinated computing and electricity demand management. During an evening electricity demand peak in August, 11 computing centers in the State Grid Jibei area released more than 100 megawatts of power supply capacity within about 10 minutes, according to Ding Cong, a senior engineer at Shanghai Post & Telecommunication Design Consulting Institute.

The project marked China's first coordinated computing and power grid adjustment on a scale exceeding 100 MW, Ding said.

In September, two data centers in Wuhan connected 15 MW of flexible electricity demand to Hubei's virtual power plant platform, completing Central China's first market-based transaction involving coordinated computing and electricity demand management.

However, the ability to adjust electricity consumption does not mean computing operations can be interrupted without restrictions. Service level agreements, thermal safety limits, and protection coordination are three boundaries that must not be breached when designing such systems, Ding stressed.

Data center operators also have limited incentives to participate in electricity demand response programs while computing capacity remains in short supply.

Companies currently prefer to maximize token output rather than reduce or shift computing activity to support the grid, said Yang Liu, an executive at Huawei's Electric Power Digitalization Business Unit.

Over the medium to long term, however, as computing capacity becomes more abundant, data centers could begin participating in electricity demand response programs and power trading according to the requirements of their computing workloads, Yang said.

Editor: Emmi Laine

data.title: Reebok Targets Up to 35 New Stores in China Next Year as US Sportswear Brand Stages Comeback, ABG Exec Says
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 23 -- Reebok, which opened its first brick-and-mortar store in China on a trial basis in Shanghai last month, plans to open between 30 and 35 stores next year as the US sportswear brand ramps up its relaunch in the country, Steve Robaire, executive vice president of Reebok at US brand management firm Authentic Brands Group, which owns the athletic footwear and apparel maker, recently told Yicai in an interview.

Reebok plans to open a second outlet in China later this year, Robaire said. The brand aims to expand its total store network in the country to 200 outlets by 2029 and achieve annual sales of USD1 billion by 2036.

The relaunch comes after a difficult few years following the sale of Reebok by German sportswear giant Adidas to New York-based ABG in 2021. ABG adopted a regional licensing model, allowing local operating partners to oversee product development, manufacturing and retail operations in their respective markets.

In 2022, Reebok’s China business was entrusted to Hong Kong’s Tristate Holdings. However, the business continued to incur losses, resulting in the closure of a large number of brick-and-mortar stores. At the end of 2025, Tristate terminated its Reebok China franchise agreement ahead of schedule.

Earlier this year, Xinrui Sports Shanghai was appointed as the principal licensee for the Reebok brand in China, paving the way for the brand’s return to the Chinese market.

Robaire sees the next six to 12 months as a critical period for the business. During this phase, the brand will focus on testing its retail model, product mix and brand positioning before accelerating its expansion.

Reebok will adopt a strategy combining “global products with locally developed offerings,” said Eva Xu, vice president of strategy at Xinrui Sports, Reebok’s partner in China. The locally developed apparel will be designed primarily by the Chinese team, subject to approval by Reebok’s global management. In the first season of locally designed products, women’s footwear accounted for 80 percent of the lineup.

Stiff Competition

However, Reebok’s return to the Chinese market comes at a time when market conditions are no less challenging than during its previous attempt.

Nike and Adidas continue to dominate the mainstream sportswear market in terms of brand recognition and consumer position, Chen Jingjing, founder of Jingjie Brand Consulting, told Yicai. Meanwhile domestic brands such as Anta and Li-Ning have built strong product offerings and distribution networks.

Competition has also intensified in specialized sports categories. On and HOKA have established strong positions in running, while Salomon has gained traction in outdoor sports. As sports consumption becomes increasingly specialized, consumers are no longer willing to buy products simply because an international brand has a long history or strong name recognition.

Reebok’s core strengths lie in its iconic footwear designs and brand heritage, Robaire said. The challenge is to make these classic products relevant and appealing to today’s consumers.

“We have built a roadmap to bring Reebok back into individual product categories through extensive research, development and product launches. We will start with running, return to competitive basketball with NBA players and then expand into global football and golf,” he said.

Legacy Challenges

The brand must address challenges inherited from the past. Towards the end of its previous operating period in China, large volumes of Reebok products flooded outlet and discount retail channels. As a result, some footwear and apparel products remained in the low-price segment for extended periods, potentially weakening the brand’s premium positioning.

The extensive discounting was linked to the transition period between Reebok’s previous China operating partner and the new partnership, Robaire said. These heavily discounted products are mainly held by third-party sellers carrying old inventory, he added.

Removing unauthorized third-party online sellers will take time, but the situation has already improved, he said. Going forward, Reebok hopes to win over consumers who are less focused on heavily discounted goods by offering new product collections, refreshed store concepts and enhanced brand communications.

Editor: Kim Taylor

data.title: CAAM to Scrutinize Supplier Payment Practices at Major Chinese Carmakers
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 17 -- The China Association of Automobile Manufacturers will evaluate supplier payment practices at 17 major domestic carmakers, including BYD and SAIC Motor, at the request of regulators seeking to standardize payment practices, shorten payment terms and promote the healthy development of the automotive industry.

CAAM has been commissioned by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology to conduct the assessment as an independent third-party organization, the industry association said yesterday. The companies under review include leading automakers such as BYD, SAIC, Dongfeng Motor Group, FAW Group and Geely Auto, as well as emerging electric vehicle manufacturers such as Xiaomi Auto, Li Auto, Nio and Xpeng.

The evaluation will be conducted annually and cover several areas, including whether automakers pay suppliers within 60 days, maintain long-term and stable supplier relationships and have built clear and effective accounts payable management systems, CAAM said. It will also examine compliance in aspects such as the proportion of payments made in cash and negotiation mechanisms.

Data will be collected through a combination of regular reporting by carmakers and random checks of selected suppliers, it said. Auto manufacturers must submit reports on their supplier payment practices for the previous calendar year by Jan. 31 each year, followed by reports covering the first half of the current year by July 31.

Over the past few years, intensifying competition in China’s automotive industry has led to increasingly extended supplier payment terms, putting pressure on the healthy development of the broader industry. Against this backdrop, 17 major Chinese carmakers jointly pledged in June last year to keep supplier payment terms within 60 days. CAAM subsequently issued an industry initiative calling on automakers to standardize their payment practices.

In September, the MIIT and the State Administration for Market Regulation rolled out new regulations aimed at standardizing carmakers’ payments to suppliers and improving payment-term management. This effectively elevated what had previously been a voluntary industry self-regulatory initiative into a formal regulatory requirement.

Over the past year, average payment terms among China’s major automakers have shortened significantly, while the proportion of payments in cash has significantly increased, resulting in an overall improvement in payment practices.

However, supplier payments involve multiple stages and practices vary considerably among carmakers. Significant challenges remain in further optimizing payment terms, and Chinese vehicle manufacturers still have room for improvement compared with established multinational automakers, an MIIT official said.

Editors: Dou Shicong, Kim Taylor

data.title: Chinese LLMs Rank First in Call Volume on OpenRouter for 30th Straight Week
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 23 -- Chinese large language models exceeded all others in combined weekly call volume on application programming interface aggregation platform OpenRouter for the 30th week in a row, with two models from DeepSeek, one of China's artificial intelligence champions, ranking first and second for the fifth consecutive week.

Global LLM call volume on OpenRouter rose 8.2 percent to 210 trillion tokens in the week ended Nov. 22 from a week earlier, according to the data the platform released today. Six of the top nine models were Chinese despite their combined volume dropping 6.7 percent to 111.16 trillion tokens.

By comparison, US models held the other three spots after their combined weekly call volume rose almost 30 percent to 19.21 trillion tokens.

DeepSeek's V4.1-Flash-1017 ranked first with 65 trillion tokens, up 16 percent from the previous week, followed by the V4.1-Flash with 15.4 trillion tokens, down 1 percent. Z.AI saw GLM-5.3-Flash's call volume climb 3 percent to 12.2 trillion tokens at third, while Tencent Holdings's newly launched Hunyuan Hy4 flash ranked fourth with 10.2 trillion tokens.

OpenRouter does not represent the entire AI model market, with its data counting only traffic routed through the platform and excluding vendors' own APIs, cloud platforms, on-premises deployments, consumer-facing apps, and web products. This means the figures cannot be directly equated with global market share.

AI models developed by Chinese firms have rapidly grown in token call volume and OpenRouter rankings over the past year, gradually becoming the main contributor to traffic. The global LLM call volume on the platform was only 7.18 trillion in the week ended Nov. 24, 2025, with MiniMax M2 the only Chinese model in the top nine.

The shift in OpenRouter's token call volume rankings highlights that Chinese models have entered users' workflows. But when it comes to paying for high-value tasks, models from global rivals remain highly competitive, resulting in monetization challenges despite the traffic lead.

Editors: Tang Shihua, Martin Kadiev

data.title: China's Offshore Oil Engineering Wins USD800 Million Contract for QatarEnergy’s MM EPIC2 Project
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 23 -- Offshore Oil Engineering, the engineering arm of state-owned offshore oil explorer China National Offshore Oil, said it secured a USD800 million contract for QatarEnergy's MM EPIC2 project, a key component of the petroleum and natural gas giant's Maydan Mahzam oilfield redevelopment plan.

Offshore Oil Engineering will oversee project management, detailed design, material procurement and transportation, construction, installation, pre-commissioning, and other related work, the Tianjin-based company announced late on Nov. 20. It will lay over 100 kilometers of offshore pipelines, cables, and umbilical cables, as well as install related facilities, with construction likely taking 66 months, it added.

The contract will affect Offshore Oil Engineering's future performance, help increase its market share in Qatar's oil field service market, and highlight strong customer recognition and high market stickiness in the country, the company pointed out, without disclosing the project's exact location and other details.

This is the second major offshore service deal Offshore Oil Engineering got from QatarEnergy or its affiliates this year, In February, an Offshore Oil Engineering consortium led by Italy's Saipem won a contract for QatarEnergy LNG's North Field offshore boosting platform and ancillary facilities worth about USD4 billion, which will boost and transport natural gas collected from surrounding wellheads through submarine pipelines built by other contractors. The Chinese firm is responsible for building the main facilities, as well as some of the design and procurement of some raw materials, securing over USD800 million of the contract share with a five-year construction period.

QatarEnergy LNG is the operating entity of QatarEnergy's liquefied natural gas business.

Shares of Offshore Oil Engineering [SHA: 600583] closed 0.5 percent higher at CNY6.26 (94 US cents) apiece today. The broader Shanghai market rose 0.2 percent.

Editor: Martin Kadiev

data.title: Tencent’s Hunyuan AI Aims to Develop Bigger Next-Gen Models Without Chasing Benchmarks Leaderboards
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 23 -- Tencent Holdings’ new Hy4 artificial intelligence model still has significant room for improvement, especially in post-training, so the Chinese internet giant’s Hunyuan team said it is investing heavily in large-scale reinforcement learning, aiming to develop a much bigger next-generation model without deliberately chasing benchmark leaderboards during training.

The parameter count of Hy4 and Hy4 flash, released earlier this month, drew particular attention during a two-hour question-and-answer session held by the Hunyuan team, including Tencent’s Chief AI Scientist Yao Shunyu, on Reddit on Nov. 21. While models from ByteDance and Kimi are pushing toward the trillion-parameter mark, Hunyuan remains at around 700 billion.

Compared with models that lean toward coding, the new Hy4 model is more geared toward general-purpose use, the team pointed out. The parameters of the next-generation Hy model are expected to expand significantly, it added.

In addition, one user pointed out that Hy4 inference sometimes takes too long.

Addressing the “overthinking” issue, the Hunyuan team said Hy4’s goal is to maximize intelligence, so overly long chains of thought are a known issue. The team noted it has distilled this capability into the more cost-effective Hy4 flash, which uses reinforcement learning to keep CoT shorter, but acknowledged that “overthinking” is the hardest behavior to fix in post-training.

Creative writing and readability are key focus areas for improvement, with room for progress in these areas, the team pointed out.

Since Yao took charge, Hunyuan abandoned the approach of chasing leaderboards through benchmark scores. Some users noted that Hunyuan has not published results on common benchmarks such as GPQA Diamond and SWE Bench.

These benchmarks were launched early on, so their scores have already saturated, the team said, adding that it instead shows results on newer, more challenging benchmarks such as Agents’ Last Exam. It also stressed that in model development, it addresses certain issues through better training data and diverse internal evaluations, without deliberately pursuing leaderboards.

On whether Hunyuan can catch up with the most cutting-edge models under restrictions on the supply of advanced AI chips, the team said it is squeezing the most out of its existing resources to reach the frontier.

Editor: Martin Kadiev

data.title: China's Computing Power Sector Faces Resource Mismatch, Experts Say
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 23 -- The computing power industry in China faces not just a question of aggregate capacity, but of allocation, with mismatches between supply and demand across different graphics processing unit models, time periods, and regions pushing the sector away from competing on compute scale and toward improving effective utilization and from leasing hardware to selling computing services, according to multiple experts.

 "Surplus and shortage of computing power exist at the same time, which is the real problem," Zheng Zheng, deputy general manager of Shanghai Science and Technology Network Communication, said at the SMM Compute Economy Summit, themed "Pricing the Intelligence," held in the city from Nov. 19 to 20. 

Zheng broke down the mismatch into three types: a GPU-type mismatch where training requires large clusters, while inference requires small instances; a temporal mismatch where capacity is tight at peak hours but sits idle off-peak, with no time-of-use pricing to balance it; and a geographic mismatch where places with cheap power lack customers, while places with customers lack power.

This means computing power is not a freely interchangeable resource, he said, adding that GPU models differ in performance, software ecosystem, interconnect capability, and suitable workloads. Even when aggregate capacity is adequate, it may not match a customer's specific training or inference needs, he noted.

The compute gap continues to widen, with demand expanding three times faster than supply, said Xie Rendong, deputy general manager of Tencent Financial Cloud.

Computing power rental surged 62 percent in the first quarter of this year from a year earlier, Xie said, noting that he expects its share of total compute supply to rise to 30 percent from 5 percent over the next three years.

There is a severe structural mismatch between compute supply and demand, said Sun Tianyin, a part-time researcher at the Center for Financial Development and Regulation Technology of Tsinghua University PBC School of Finance and founder of Ruiyi Digital Technology. Computing power and renewable energy face spatial and temporal mismatches, Sun added, noting that flexibly adjusting the execution time and nodes of computing tasks while meeting delivery constraints can improve computing power utilization and promote renewable energy consumption.

From 'Racked' to 'Effectively Used'

Amid this mismatch, the standard for measuring computing power is changing, and parameter size no longer equals actual consumption, Xie said. The race for scale is becoming a race for efficiency, Xie added.

Compute utilization should be measured on rack-up, allocation, and effective utilization rates, according to Zheng. A GPU being racked and allocated to a customer does not mean it is steadily completing productive tasks, meaning effective utilization should be the ultimate metric, he noted.

Delivery assessments should also shift from "data center available" to "workload available," measured by the number of days from contract signing to the stable operation of the first production task, he said. On energy efficiency, he proposed replacing power usage effectiveness with tokens per watt, or the number of effective tokens generated per watt, as the key indicator.

"The value of computing power lies not in peak capacity, but in how many productive tasks it can run steadily," Zheng stressed.

From Selling Resources to Services

Traditional internet data centers are moving from pure rack leasing to integrated services combining "racks + bandwidth + operations & maintenance," as well as usage-based artificial intelligence compute services, Zheng said. Pricing can adopt a hybrid model combining long-term contract baseload, on-demand elasticity, and reserved capacity, he added.

Companies need more than a one-off model call, Sun said, adding that they need manageable AI services suited to their own businesses that they can use continuously. 

Inference compute services could be priced per request, said Yuan Zhonghua, president of the Alumni International Exchange Association at Shanghai Jiao Tong University's Antai College of Economics and Management. "Sell results, not resources."

Inference service pricing is increasingly tied to usage and output, not just the underlying hardware. More transparent pricing also helps improve resource allocation. 

SMM released a computing power rental price index at the conference, providing reference prices for rental prices across GPU models.

Editor: Martin Kadiev

data.title: China Takes Steps to Speed Up Third-Generation Nuclear Power Rollout
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 6 -- China is seeking to accelerate the introduction of its proprietary third-generation nuclear power technology by improving reactor design, digitizing project management, speeding up equipment production, and harmonizing technical standards. The push also involves bringing private investors into projects to widen the funding base and bolster the domestic supply chain.

China General Nuclear Power Group unveiled the Hualong One 2.0, a third-generation pressurized water reactor, in September, featuring improvements in safety, cost-effectiveness, and technological performance.

The upgraded reactor design is intended to boost the efficiency of both project management and construction by 20 percent, with the overall building period capped at 54 months, according to Kan Shuo, deputy director of the Project Management Engineering Technology Support Centre at China Nuclear Engineering Corporation.

At the end of last year, the generating capacity of nuclear power units in commercial operation in China was 62.5 million kilowatts, less than 2 percent of the nation’s total electricity production capacity. This leaves a significant gap to cover to reach the 200-million-kilowatt target projected by the China Nuclear Energy Association for 2040.

Addressing the pressure to meet delivery timelines, Kan noted that in February, China National Nuclear Corporation proposed integrating digital engineering concepts into the design-and-construction process. This allows for seamless flow of data across different project sectors, with the goal of achieving a 20 percent improvement in both management and construction efficiency, and capping the total project duration at 54 months.

The initial delivery estimate for a Hualong One 2.0 reactor was nearly 50 months, said Liu Chang, project management director at First Heavy Industries Dalian Nuclear Power & Petrochemical, a firm responsible for equipment manufacturing. But through process refinement, the delivery time is now expected to be just over 40 months, Liu noted.

Private Capital

In terms of capital, China has begun introducing private investment into nuclear power projects. The San'ao Nuclear Power Plant in Zhejiang province is the first to have private equity participation. The plant is set to have six 1,000-megawatt Hualong One units, with a total projected investment of CNY120 billion (USD17.9 billion).
 

Private investors have a 2 percent stake in the project's first phase, a figure that rises to 30 percent by the third phase, setting a record for the most private funding in China’s nuclear power sector. 

"The participation of private capital has become a key prerequisite for the approval of certain nuclear power projects,” said Xu Lingbin, deputy manager of general management at Cangnan Nuclear Power, which is responsible for building and running the San'ao Nuclear Power Plant.

“Private capital helps supplement the substantial equity funding required for these projects, and private enterprises with strong industrial backgrounds can foster synergy across the upstream and downstream supply chains," Xu told Yicai.

Unified Standards

Efforts are also underway to harmonize standards to facilitate faster project implementation. China’s two major nuclear power conglomerates, CGN and CNNC, previously used different technical standards. 

Efforts to harmonize standards began in 2017, but the alignment did not include a number of equipment components. As of 2024, atomic power industry regulators have pushed for further standardization, encompassing the entire project lifecycle, from design and construction to operation and decommissioning. 

"Promoting the unification of standards is a positive development for the manufacturing sector,” said Gao Dianbao, executive deputy general manager of First Heavy Industries Dalian Nuclear Power, which supplies equipment to both CGN and CNNC. “It streamlines processes and helps unlock production capacity," Gao added.

Editor: Tom Litting

data.title: Shanghai Metals Market Launches Computing Power Rental Price Index
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 23 -- Shanghai Metals Market, a leading Chinese provider of price reporting, data, and intelligence on the nonferrous and ferrous metals industry, has released a computing power rental price index, aiming to set a unified price reference for the fragmented and highly non-standardized computing power rental market in China.

China's computing power rental market suffers from inconsistent hardware specifications, scattered transactions, opaque actual transaction prices, and mixed pricing bases, Liu Xiaolei, chief analyst of SMM's artificial intelligence computing power division, said at the SMM Compute Economy Summit, titled "Pricing the Intelligence Age" and held from Nov. 19 to 20. The index, launched at the event, is designed to lower transaction costs for buyers and sellers and provide an impartial third-party price reference, Liu pointed out.

The SMM Computing Power Rental Spot Price Index and spot list prices have been updated daily since July 3, while the composite price index has been published every trading day since Sept. 21, according to the website of SMM.

The new index adopts a two-tier structure. The first uses a combination of "card model × region × lease term" as the stock-keeping unit, publishing daily low, volume-weighted average, and high prices, while the second introduces the standard computing unit, using the Nvidia H100 as the equivalent computing power benchmark, converting prices across graphics processing units into a weighted composite, quoted in Chinese yuan per card-hour.

The index covers bare-metal whole servers in the Chinese mainland, incorporating mainstream GPUs including the H100, A100, H20, Huawei Ascend 910B series, and RTX 4090. Standardized delivery terms are defined for server configuration, electricity, bandwidth, minimum lease requirements, and delivery lead time to remove noise from non-standard factors.

Similar moves have been made overseas. The Silicon Data H100 Rental Index, released by New York-based startup Silicon Data, went live on the Bloomberg terminal, with futures and derivatives exchange firm CME Group planning to launch compute futures based on the index, but the listing has been postponed to next year because of an extended review by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

Carmen Li, founder of Silicon Data, delivered a keynote speech at the SMM Compute Economy Summit.

On Nov. 20, the SMM Computing Power Rental Composite Price Index stood at 16.535 yuan per card-hour, while the composite token price index was 13.495 yuan per million tokens, according to SMM's website. Card-hours measure the cost of renting computing resources, while tokens more closely reflect the actual output of AI inference services, with the two pricing methods running in parallel.

AI model call volume in China reached 119.1 trillion tokens on application programming interface aggregation platform OpenRouter in the week ended Nov. 15, outpacing the US for the 29th consecutive week, Ao Li, vice president of the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, said at the conference.

SMM has branches and offices in nine countries and regions and hopes to build on this network to create a globally covered analytics platform, enhancing China's pricing power, a senior executive from the company told Yicai.

SMM's metal spot benchmark prices have undergone independent assurance under the International Organization of Securities Commissions' Principles for Financial Benchmarks and are used by supply chain companies as spot settlement references, industry insiders said, noting that applying this methodology to computing power has the advantage of reusing an established price-collection network and industry trust. However, the challenge is that computing power is far less standardized than metals, they pointed out.

Editor: Martin Kadiev

data.title: China Expands List of Flagship Smart Factories in Industrial AI Drive
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 20 -- China has added 34 plants to a list of flagship smart factories, bringing the total number to 49, as the the world's biggest manufacturing country forges ahead with embedding artificial intelligence across industrial production.

The updated list of pioneer-level smart factories, the highest tier in China’s four-tier smart factory program, was released yesterday by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and several other government departments.

Pioneer smart factories deeply integrate AI into daily operations and explore innovative manufacturing paradigms, with the potential to develop into globally competitive industry benchmarks. To this end, they get special government backing, including expert technical guidance, resource matching, and public services support.

The ministry said that over 70 percent of operations at plants in the second batch added to the list use AI. Collectively, these facilities have developed in excess of 1,000 industrial AI agents, averaging more than 300 million token calls a day.

AI adoption at these factories is expanding rapidly from auxiliary operations to core areas such as research and development, design, process optimization, and production. They have also helped nearly 4,000 upstream and downstream enterprises carry out digital and intelligent upgrading, according to the ministry.

For example, the ultra-high voltage transformer smart factory operated by TBEA in Hengyang, Hunan province, has deployed 69 AI models and 35 industrial agents, with AI now covering 87 percent of its operational scenarios.

A traditional Chinese medicine plant run by Tasly Pharmaceutical Group in Tianjin is the only pharmaceutical production base that has so far been designated a pioneer smart factory. Addressing industry pain points such as the complexity of TCM herbal ingredients and the difficulty of quality control, Tasly has developed its own production line, which enables traceability and optimization across the entire production process.

Under the smart factory classification system, the other tiers are: basic -- factories that use digital data collection and connectivity for key processes; advanced -- factories that allow for data interoperability across business functions and coordinate production, supply, and sales, serving as regional industry benchmarks; and excellence -- factories that achieve full-chain data integration and systematic intelligent optimization, serving as national industry benchmarks.

Ministry statistics show that China now has in excess of 60,000 at the basic level, more than 13,000 at the advanced level, and over 750 at the excellence level.

Editors: Tang Shihua, Tom Litting

data.title: China's Smaller Airports Face Funding Scrutiny as Passenger Numbers Plunge
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 20 -- As production of Alibaba Group Holding’s own artificial intelligence chips cranks up, the Chinese technology giant expects to grow the share of domestic computing power it uses, making it an increasingly important revenue driver for the group’s cloud computing arm, its chief executive officer has said.

“Progress in developing domestic computing power has exceeded out expectations,” Eddie Wu said on the Hangzhou-based company’s third-quarter earnings conference call late yesterday.

Alibaba, which set up its chip unit T-Head Semiconductor in 2018, is already using its proprietary AI chips to train the next-generation Qwen large language model and expects them to fully support ultra-large-scale model training by the first quarter of next year, he added.

After 2027, the bulk of Alibaba’s AI chip supplies will likely come from T-Head, whose flagship products will be prioritized for developing and upgrading models at Alibaba and its key strategic partners, he noted. For AI inference workloads, the company will buy more chips of different types, including from other domestic producers, he added.

The e-commerce giant’s multi-year pivot to AI has become the centerpiece of its growth strategy, with the focus increasingly shifting to monetization to drive earnings amid vast spending across the entire technology stack. In May, Wu said Alibaba would overshoot the CNY380 billion (USD57 billion) investment in AI over the next five years that it had announced in February last year.

Alibaba is moving past the period of heaviest investment in AI infrastructure, he said yesterday. As China’s computing supply chain scales up and shifts away from a heavy reliance on external chip procurement, profit margins at Alibaba’s cloud and AI businesses will likely improve significantly by 2028, Wu said.

The AI industry is still in its early stages, with varying opinions on whether applications or models matter more, Wu said. Alibaba’s strategy is to develop both at the same time, he noted, adding that in the long run, he is more optimistic about integrated solutions that combine models with specific use cases to deliver unique value to customers.

Alibaba Cloud has a revenue growth target for the fiscal year starting April of 30 percent to 45 percent, Wu said. However, as domestic computing power use increases, the subsidiary will likely resume high-speed growth of more than 50 percent in the second half of 2028, he noted.

Alibaba’s net profit more than tripled to CNY64.5 billion (USD9.7 billion) in the fiscal quarter ended Sept. 30 from a year earlier, while revenue rose 10 percent to CNY271.5 billion (USD40.7 billion). AI-related income posted triple-digit growth for the 13th straight quarter, but free cash flow ended at a CNY34.5 billion outflow due to massive cloud infrastructure investments.

Alibaba’s shares [HKG: 9988] closed 3.5 percent higher at HKD83.35 (USD10.63) each in Hong Kong today, after ending 5.5 percent lower yesterday. Its New York-listed stock [NYSE: BABA] was trading up 1.1 percent as of 5.51 a.m. local time today, after declining 1.3 percent yesterday.

Editors: Tang Shihua, Martin Kadiev

data.title: NetEase Shares Plummet as Gaming Revenue Falls, Short Dramas Take Toll
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 20 -- Shares of Chinese gaming giant NetEase tanked after it reported a rare decrease in gaming revenue in the third quarter, with its chief executive acknowledging that the short-drama boom has hurt the business.

Hangzhou-based NetEase's US-listed shares [NASDAQ: NTES] sank 11.4 percent to USD104.94 following the earnings release yesterday, while its Hong Kong-listed stock [HK: 9999] tumbled 17.6 percent to HKD154 (USD19.60) today.

Net profit fell almost 3 percent from a year earlier to CNY8.4 billion (USD1.3 billion) in the three months ended Sept. 30, while revenue dropped 2 percent to CNY27.9 billion (USD4.2 billion), according to the earnings report. Revenue from games and value-added services, NetEase's largest business segment, slipped 2 percent to CNY22.9 billion.

Short dramas have experienced explosive growth this year, attracting significant user attention and affecting games in the short term, Ding said during an earnings call. Over the longer term, however, the two offer different entertainment experiences, with games appealing to users through control and feedback, while short dramas rely primarily on storytelling, he added.

The decrease in NetEase's third-quarter gaming revenue exposed the growth pressure the company faces during a gap in new product launches, securities research firm Dolphin Research said in a note.

With short dramas competing for users' time and competition intensifying in the gaming market, NetEase can no longer rely solely on its established evergreen titles to sustain its previous growth pace, Dolphin added.

AI Opens New Opportunities

Ding believes the development of AI has not only fueled the rapid rise of short dramas but also created new possibilities for game developers. Gameplay mechanics and creative concepts that were previously difficult to implement are becoming feasible, including interactive film-style games.

NetEase is already exploring this type of content. Earlier this month, it launched Tianma, a standalone app offering short dramas and AI-powered interactive stories that let viewers shape the plot and choose different endings at key moments.

NetEase's other businesses delivered mixed results in the third quarter. Revenue from NetEase Cloud Music edged down 1 percent from a year earlier to CNY1.9 billion, while revenue from its online education arm Youdao fell 12 percent to CNY1.4 billion, according to the earnings report. Revenue from innovative and other businesses rose 7 percent to CNY1.5 billion.

Editors: Dou Shicong, Emmi Laine

data.title: China's Virtual Power Plant Capacity Jumps Over 60% to Beat 2027 Target
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 20 -- China's virtual power plant regulation capacity surged more than 60 percent from a year earlier to more than 20 million kilowatts as of the end of June, beating a national target for 2027 a year ahead of schedule.

China had more than 590 virtual power plants in operation as of June 30, up 79 percent from a year earlier, according to a report released by the National Energy Administration yesterday. Their combined maximum regulation capacity reached 20.4 million kilowatts, an increase of 63 percent, exceeding the target set in March 2025 for 2027. 

The milestone comes as China seeks to make its power grid more flexible. Instead of building new generating stations, virtual power plants pool resources such as energy storage systems, adjustable electricity loads and electric vehicle chargers to help balance supply and demand and participate in electricity trading.

The country aims to increase the regulation capacity of virtual power plants to 50 million kW by 2030, according to a target announced by the National Development and Reform Commission and the NEA in June.

Private companies are playing a major role in the sector's expansion. They had invested in and built nearly 270 virtual power plants as of the end of June, accounting for 45 percent of the national total, the latest report showed.

The average investment in a virtual power plant is about CNY300 (USD45) per kW of regulation capacity, an industry insider told Yicai. By comparison, building a single one-million-kW coal-fired power generating unit in Shanghai would involve substantial costs associated with energy consumption quotas, land requirements and coal supply arrangements, the person said.

At the national level, developing the equivalent of 50 million kW of regulation capacity through conventional thermal power generation would require more than CNY100 billion (USD15 billion) in investment, according to the industry insider.

Investors in virtual power plants include electricity retailers and companies operating electric vehicle charging and battery-swapping facilities. Private enterprises have financed more than half of the virtual power plants operating in Shanghai and the provinces of Jiangsu and Guangdong.

Editor: Emmi Laine

data.title: China to Welcome 200 Million Foreign Tourists in Next Five Years, Trip.Com’s Chair Says
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 20 -- About 200 million international tourists are expected to visit China over the next five years, according to the co-founder and chairman of Chinese online travel agency Trip.Com Group.

In response to the increasing number of foreign tourists in China, Trip.Com plans to increase investment and spend over CNY10 billion (USD1.5 billion) on related promotional campaigns, Liang Jianzhang said at a corporate event held yesterday.

China registered more than 34.5 million foreign arrivals in the first three quarters of the year, up about 19 percent from a year earlier, according to the latest data from the National Immigration Administration. Visa-free entries accounted for more than 77 percent of the total, up about 24 percent in the period.

“Tailor-made travel is one of the future development directions of the Chinese inbound tourism market,” Wei Meiling, general manager of the Hefei branch of Zhongji International Travel Service, told Yicai. “Today, travelers’ willingness to pay has shifted from ‘hardware luxury’ to ‘exclusive experiences.’”

In the past, tourists focused more on staying in five-star hotels or riding in luxury vehicles, but now more and more are willing to pay a premium for exclusive local experiences, such as private after-hours museum tours and bespoke dinners, Wei explained. “Such in-depth products built around a sense of participation and exclusivity are becoming the core competitiveness of high-end, tailor-made travel.”

Themed travel that integrates culture, commerce, tourism, sports, and exhibitions holds greater potential in cross-border markets. “Going forward, wellness and sports tourism driven by events and experiences will grow at a rate of 8 percent to 10 percent, while cultural tourism incorporating theater and music festivals can grow at a pace of more than 10 percent,” Liang predicted.

Both Chinese tourist visits to Australia and Australian tourist visits to China expanded between July last year and June this year, Trip.Com’s Chief Executive Officer Jane Sun said at the same event yesterday. On Trip.Com’s overseas platforms, Australian travelers to China grew about 14 percent in the period from a year earlier.

Trip.Com and its Australian partners will implement a unified promotional strategy to activate tourist flows in both directions, leveraging Trip.Com’s overseas platforms to bring more Australians to China for in-depth travel, while making early arrangements for tourism products related to the 2032 Brisbane Olympic Games, turning international sports events into global tourism opportunities.

Editor: Futura Costaglione

data.title: China’s Changan Auto to Sell 10% Stake in EV Brand Avatr for at Least USD479.7 Million
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 13 -- China’s Changan Automobile is seeking to sell a 10 percent stake in its electric vehicle brand Avatr Technology, which is moving ahead with a Hong Kong initial public offering amid shrinking sales and cash reserves, for a minimum of CNY3.2 billion (USD479.7 million).

Changan will list just over 306.5 million Avatr shares for sale on the Shanghai United Assets and Equity Exchange, with the disclosure period running through Dec. 10, the state-owned carmaker announced yesterday. Avatr has a valuation floor of CNY31.8 billion (USD4.8 billion), about in line with its post-money valuation after its Series C funding round in December 2024.

The buyer must pay a CNY500 million (USD75 million) deposit and settle the full purchase price within three working days of signing the equity transfer contract, Changan noted. It must also guarantee that the source of funds is legal and compliant, that the transaction will not hinder Avatr’s IPO, and that it has no competing business with the brand.

The buyer will be expected to provide support mainly in areas such as premium brand sales channel development and overseas market expansion, Changan told Yicai. After the deal closes, the Chongqing-based carmaker will continue backing Avatr in core areas including technology research and development, vehicle manufacturing, and supply chain, it added.

If the entire 10 percent stake is acquired by a single buyer, it would become Avatr’s second-largest shareholder. Changan owns about 41 percent of Avatr, making it the largest shareholder, followed by battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology with around 9.2 percent. 

Avatr sold 20,160 vehicles from January through May, according to its IPO prospectus. China Passenger Car Association data shows its domestic retail sales dropped below 3,000 last month. Its cash on hand fell to about CNY6.2 billion in late April from CNY9.7 billion on Dec. 31 and CNY19.3 billion at the end of 2024, implying an average monthly burn rate of more than CNY800 million.

For yet-to-be-profitable automakers listed in Hong Kong, sales expectations affect revenue growth and the price-to-sales ratio, while cash reserves and the cash burn rate relate to a company's cash runway, a key metric watched by capital market investors, industry experts told Yicai.

Changan’s shares [SHE: 000625] closed 0.3 percent lower at CNY6.88 (US1.03) each today, while the wider Shenzhen market shed 2.1 percent. The stock has fallen 42 percent so far this year.

Editor: Martin Kadiev

data.title: US' NSF Opens USD8 Million Shanghai Lab to Help Local Water Gear Exporters Get 'Global Passport'
data.description:
(Yicai) Nov. 20 -- NSF has opened a USD8 million physical testing laboratory in Shanghai, marking the US public health and safety organization's largest single investment in China and enabling local producers of water equipment like purifiers to complete export certifications without shipping prototypes overseas.

The NSF China Physical Mechanical Laboratory, covering more than 3,000 square meters, is located in Minhang district's Pujiang Town next to the firm's Chinese chemistry lab, which opened in 2011. The two facilities can conduct all physical and chemical testing required for the company's water product certifications.

The new lab is NSF's first wholly owned facility outside the United States capable of testing drinking water treatment systems, while its two Shanghai labs are the first in the Asia-Pacific region to conduct Water Regulations Approval Scheme approval testing under the UK's Regulation 4.

Pedro Sancha, president and chief executive officer of NSF, said the project is "probably the biggest investment we made in a laboratory for NSF, building from the ground up worldwide" since he took the helm.

With Chinese exporters increasingly diversifying beyond traditional US and European strongholds into Southeast Asia and Latin America, NSF is positioning itself as a single "global passport" for multi-market compliance, he noted, adding that the firm's certification is mandatory for water products in markets including the US and Canada, with its standards written into regulations in many other countries.

"We can help the Chinese manufacturers navigate complex regulatory landscapes and be their single partner to export to all these different markets," he pointed out.

Since entering China in 2005, NSF has built a base of several thousand local clients, part of its 40,000 global roster across more than 110 countries and regions.

The China business has posted double-digit annual growth for the past eight to nine years, despite the Covid-19 pandemic and US trade tensions, noted John Shan, managing director of NSF's country arm. The new lab is a key investment under the firm's 2030 growth strategy, with China as a priority region, he added.

Bridging Trust Deficit

For Chinese producers of water purifiers, valves, and piping, speed to market is a defining competitive edge, and cross-border testing has long been a bottleneck, with manufacturers typically rolling out a new generation of products every two to four years, while a product line in the US or Europe can sell for 20 years, Shan pointed out. Shipping bulky prototypes to NSF labs in the US or the United Kingdom meant lengthy logistics delays, along with time-zone and language barriers, he said.

The Shanghai facility is slated to receive its first test samples by year-end and ramp up operations in early next year. By bringing testing to China, NSF aims to pull regulatory compliance upstream into the research and development phase rather than leaving it as the last step in product development.

"The lab shortens not only testing time, but also the time it takes for companies' innovations to reach the market, the time needed to prepare products for international markets, and the distance between R&D innovation and commercial success," said Yu Zhiyong, general manager of water business at NSF China.

Beyond logistics, certification helps Chinese exporters overcome a persistent trust deficit abroad, with Shan pointing to domestic water purifier maker Angel, whose executives said the hardest part of going overseas was not product strength or technology, but winning foreign markets' trust. Once the Shenzhen-based firm secured NSF certification for its core lineup, breaking into overseas hospital, school, and retail supply chains became markedly easier, he said.

Shanghai Speed and Reverse Innovation

Building the new lab also shows how NSF is tapping Chinese engineering speed and domestic equipment suppliers.

Within six months of Sancha's visit to the Minhang site, the local team had completed the build-out, installed testing lines, and obtained the necessary accreditations. Rather than relying solely on imported Western machinery, NSF turned to domestic vendors for core hardware.

During a tour of the facility, Shan revealed that a custom automated system spiked water with pollutants and measured filter removal rates. Working with a Chinese equipment maker, NSF took the system from design to commissioning in about four months.

Inside the facility, which is kept at a constant 25 degrees Celsius, automated rigs simulate tens of thousands of button presses and faucet turns to verify mechanical durability.

In addition, the Shanghai team has upgraded some equipment functions and will share its experience with NSF's global lab network, the company said.

From PFAS to 'Plastic Taste'

Alongside export certification, the Shanghai hub anchors NSF's push to shape standards for the Chinese market.

Social media-savvy younger consumers in China and abroad are scrutinizing product claims more closely than ever, exposing brands to greater reputational risk, Sancha pointed out, noting that consumers are "more aware of what they put in their bodies" and want what is on the label to match what is in the bottle.

Over the past couple of years, NSF has developed two drinking-water protocols tailored to Chinese consumer pain points: NSF P535, which evaluates how effectively purifiers remove contaminants of public concern, such as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, and NSF P558, a sensory benchmark testing taste and odor, directly addressing local consumers' complaints that filtered water can carry a "plastic taste."

"It's both supporting going global as well as the high-quality development strategies here in China," Sancha said.

While the Shanghai lab's first phase focuses on residential and commercial water products, a second phase may expand into food equipment, Shan added.

Editor: Martin Kadiev
